To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we present the first tight runtime bound for the synchronous gathering problem of autonomous robots in the plane with limited visibility.

(i) for any fixed constant viewing range r, the robots can gather in O(n^3) rounds; (ii) for a fixed viewing range r, there exists a constant c>0 such that the robots can gather if and only if r> c; and (iii) for any viewing range r, a lower bound of Omega(n^2) rounds is known.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following problem: Given a set R of n robots with unit disk graphs G1,...,Gn and an integer k, can we guarantee that all robots of R meet in one point within k steps?
gathering algorithms for synchronous robots with a fixed viewing range that are local and keep the unit disk graph connected.
the question of whether it is possible to achieve a gathering of the robots in a finite amount of time and how much time is needed to gather the robots.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the problem is not solvable in time O(n^2) and that there is an algorithm which solves the problem in time O(n^{3+\epsilon}), where \epsilon>0 is an arbitrarily small constant.
the problem is solvable in O(n^2) time and O(n) space.
for the gathering problem in the synchronous model no better bound than O(n3) exists for local algorithms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the runtime for gathering is Θ(n ^{2} log n) in the worst case, but that this bound can be significantly improved for many interesting classes of input graphs.
we provide a very tight upper bound on the runtime of local gathering algorithms for robots in the Euclidian plane, which is optimal up to a factor of O(logn).
in this setting the runtime of gathering n robots in the Euclidian plane is O(n3).
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in contrast to the previously best known bound of O(n^4) steps, a runtime bound of only O(n^3 log^3 n) steps suffices to solve this gathering problem.
